title: Ῥοιὰ καὶ μηλέα καὶ ἐλαία καὶ βάτος
titleEn: The Pomegranate, the Apple Tree, the Olive and the Bramble
part: The Pomegranate, the Apple Tree, the Olive and the Bramble (Chambry 324)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 324. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ῥοιὰ καὶ μηλέα καὶ ἐλαία περὶ εὐκαρπίας ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Rhoia kai mēlea kai elaia peri eukarpias ērizon.
sentences.l: A pomegranate and an apple tree and an olive were quarrelling about fruitfulness.
sentences.i: A pomegranate, an apple tree and an olive were quarrelling over which of them bore the finer fruit.
sentences.n: ἐρίζω περί with the genitive is to contend about a thing. εὐκαρπία is bearing good fruit, not merely much of it. All three trees are feminine nouns, which is why the bramble can address them as φίλαι below.

sentences.t: Πολλοῦ δὲ τοῦ νείκους ἀναφθέντος, βάτος ἐκ τοῦ πλησίον φραγμοῦ ἀκούσασα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ φίλαι, παυσώμεθά ποτε μαχόμεναι. »
sentences.tr: Pollou de tou neikous anaphthentos, batos ek tou plēsion phragmou akousasa eipen· « All’, ō philai, pausōmetha pote machomenai. »
sentences.l: And a great quarrel having been kindled, a bramble from the neighbouring hedge, having heard, said: « Come, friends, let us cease fighting at last. »
sentences.i: When the quarrel had blazed up high, a bramble in the hedge close by heard them and said: « Come, my friends, let us stop fighting at last. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute again, with ἀναφθέντος from ἀνάπτω, 'to kindle': the quarrel is a fire that has caught. παύομαι takes a supplementary participle for what one leaves off — μαχόμεναι, 'fighting' — and παυσώμεθα is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us cease'. ἀλλά at the head of an appeal is 'come now'. The whole joke is in the first person plural: the bramble was no party to the quarrel and quietly enrols itself among the fruit trees.

sentences.t: Οὕτω παρὰ τὰς τῶν ἀμεινόνων στάσεις καὶ οἱ μηδενὸς ἄξιοι πειρῶνται δοκεῖν τι εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Houtō para tas tōn ameinonōn staseis kai hoi mēdenos axioi peirōntai dokein ti einai.
sentences.l: Thus, amid the dissensions of their betters, even those worth nothing try to seem to be something.
sentences.i: Thus, when their betters fall out, even those who are worth nothing try to pass for persons of consequence.
sentences.n: παρά with the accusative here is 'in the course of, at the time of'. στάσις is the falling-out of a party or a city into factions. καί before οἱ μηδενὸς ἄξιοι is 'even'. δοκεῖν τι εἶναι, 'to seem to be something', is the same idiom as δοκοῦσί τινες εἶναι at fable 95, where worthless men likewise make their moment out of other people's disturbances.
